title: Bhandari: ceremonial service and changing livelihoods
description: Bhandari community history in Odisha through life-cycle services, remuneration, regional names, wedding practices, salons and ceremonial bands.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy
lead: A community history needs to follow relationships as well as occupations. For Bhandari history in Odisha, the questions include who performed ceremonial work, how that work was supported, and how families found new livelihoods.

sections.title: Women and men in ceremonial work

paragraphs.text: The Bhadrak District Gazetteer describes Bhandari, locally also called Barika or Napita, through services at births, marriages and deaths. It explicitly includes women as well as men. Its account of village-deity worship also names Bhandari among communities whose members could serve at shrines. These passages make ceremonial participation part of the history, alongside hair cutting.
The account leaves the women unnamed and their tasks briefly described. Attributed local accounts could recover contributions that a general occupational label conceals.

Bhadrak describes payment in cash and kind, and tax-free land provided for services. It reports that such land had subsequently been settled in barbers’ names and that some had opened salons. This is the gazetteer’s description of changing arrangements, not evidence from individual land grants inspected here.
Its broad claim that the jajman relationship had disappeared should be read as the author’s assessment. It cannot establish the end of every patron–service relationship across Odisha.

sections.title: A name explanation and a wedding account

paragraphs.text: In the 1909 Bhondari entry, Edgar Thurston quotes S. P. Rice’s explanation connecting the name with treasure and barbers entrusted with guarding zamindars’ treasuries. An explanation of a name does not establish when a caste formed or identify a founding event.

The same regional account describes women making ulu cries, wedding parties collecting water from seven houses, and the newly married couple and relatives throwing turmeric water on the fifth day. The sequence matters: this is an early description of a particular wedding practice, not proof that every present-day event called Haldi has the same history.
Protecting local heritage calls for that level of detail: the place, participants, name and timing of a custom, with changes traced rather than assumed.

The Ganjam District Gazetteer describes Telugu barbers, called Mangali and locally Telenga Bhandari, separately from Odia barbers. Its use of related labels does not establish one shared community identity everywhere. Nor can a surname or the fact that someone cuts hair establish that person’s caste.

The account describes Telugu barbers organising bands that played popular film songs at social and religious functions, and Odia barbers taking up band work too. It also reports salons replacing household visits, particularly in towns. These are specific observations about changing work; the passage does not provide dates or a current survey of the practice.

The band example gives us a useful way to investigate cultural change: who learned a repertoire, who requested it, and how it supported a livelihood. Establishing whether an older local practice was displaced would need further evidence. The sources here do not settle that question, or establish a single origin for the community.
